timeline.event: High unemployment, inflation, and double-digit interest rates create pressure on builders to complete fast-tracked projects swiftly.
Construction begins on the 40-story Hyatt Regency Kansas City.
A total of 2,700 square feet (250 m2) of the hotel roof collapses.
Havens Steel Company proposes using two separate and offset sets of rods instead of the single continuous rods in the original design.
Engineer Daniel M. Duncan accepts Havens Steel's proposed plan via a phone call without performing necessary calculations or viewing sketches.
Onsite workers notice beams bending and reroute their heavy wheelbarrows around the unsteady walkways without reporting it.
The Hyatt Regency Kansas City officially opens.
The fourth-floor walkway drops several inches, pauses, and crashes down onto the second-floor walkway, causing both to fall onto the crowded lobby floor during a tea dance.
Wayne G. Lischka discovers a change to the original walkway design, and a laboratory at Lehigh University begins testing box beams.
The Hyatt Regency reopens following atrium redesigns after a committee of engineers and architects concludes there are no other structural safety issues.
The Kansas City Star and the Kansas City Times win a Pulitzer Prize for their 16 months of investigative coverage of the collapse.
Local authorities report that the $5 million hotel reconstruction makes the building possibly the safest in the country.
The Hyatt disaster is cited in arguments against the Reagan administration's attempt to eliminate an agency of the National Bureau of Standards.
The hotel is renamed the Hyatt Regency Crown Center.

legacy.what: The hotel atrium was redesigned, replacing the second-floor walkway with one supported by columns, permanently removing the other walkways, and reinforcing the roof.
The Kansas City Star and the Kansas City Times won a Pulitzer Prize for their investigative coverage of the collapse.
The disaster was cited in arguments against the Reagan administration's attempt to eliminate an agency of the National Bureau of Standards.
The hotel was renamed the Hyatt Regency Crown Center.
The American Society of Civil Engineers adopted a policy making structural engineers ultimately responsible for reviewing fabricators' shop drawings.
The Kansas City Codes Administration was turned into its own department, doubling its staff and assigning a single engineer comprehensively to all aspects of each reviewed building.
